Spanish driving theory · Category B (cars) · DGT exam

Topic 10 · Accidents and their factors

Original study notes that follow the order of your course’s Topic 10. The wording and the diagrams are our own; the rules come from the Ley sobre Tráfico and the Reglamento General de Circulación, including the October 2026 reform for vulnerable road users (RD 518/2026), and the DGT’s instruction on driver-assistance systems, as they stand in November 2026.

What this topic is really about
  • Why accidents happen and how to avoid them: who runs the most risk (vulnerable road users and young drivers), and the three factors — the driver (70–90 %), the road and its surroundings (10–35 %) and the vehicle (4–13 %).
  • The exam loves numbers: reaction time 0.75 s, a break every 2 h or 200 km for 20–30 min, alcohol 0.25 / 0.15 / 0 mg/l, tread 1.6 mm, child seats up to 135 cm, head-restraint gap 4 cm, airbag 25 cm, braking distance ×2 in rain and ×10 on ice.
  • It includes the rules in force since 1 October 2026 (RD 518/2026): e-scooter riders must be 15 and wear a helmet; every cyclist wears a helmet out of town; motorcyclists need gloves out of town and closed shoes; delivery riders wear a vest at all times.
  • The sections follow the order of your course’s Topic 10. Spanish exam terms are in italics in the English text, and a glossary closes the topic.

1The social impact of accidents

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), road accidents are a serious, priority public-health problem all over the world, and in Spain they are one of the main causes of death and injury. Besides the human side, they bring other major costs that all citizens bear, directly or indirectly — each death affects about 100 people on average.

CostWhat it includes
HumanYears of life and of working capacity lost; physical and psychological suffering of the victim, family and friends.
MaterialDamage to vehicles, load, the road, its surroundings and the environment.
HealthFirst aid, care and treatment of the injured, rehabilitation and adaptations for those hurt.
AdministrativePolice and fire services, insurance and other services; legal costs.

People are rarely well informed about the real size of the problem and tend to underestimate it. Cutting accidents and their consequences takes a responsible attitude, good road-safety knowledge and driving with the greatest safety at all times.

1.1 Accidents can be avoided

Most accidents can be avoided. They are not chance or bad luck: they are predictable events caused by circumstances that make them more likely — the risk factors. The key is to avoid them, especially the ones that depend on the driver.

Risk factors that depend on…How to avoid them
The driver (the most important)Unsuitable speed, distractions, fatigue, sleep, illness, medicines, alcohol, drugs…
The vehicleInvest in safety, follow the manufacturer’s maintenance, pass the ITV: avoid mechanical failures.
The road and its surroundingsAdapt your speed to the circumstances, keep the safety distance, take the weather into account.

2Where and when accidents happen

The most dangerous places
Accidents with victims (dead and injured): more on urban roads. Deaths: more on interurban roads (carreteras), because speeds are higher.
Most accidents on interurban roads happen on straight stretches with good visibility, by running off the road — single-vehicle accidents, where it is easier to get distracted.
Autovías and autopistas are the safest roads: separate carriageways, no intersections, a gentler layout.
The most dangerous times
Going to and leaving work, especially at the end of the working day in the afternoon.
Holidays, public holidays and weekends, especially in the early hours (madrugada).
Vans: the key figures
  • Most van accidents happen between 7:00 and 23:59; the worst hour is 15:00–16:00. The worst day is Friday, then Monday.
  • More accidents on urban roads, but more deaths on interurban roads.
  • Most common factor: driver distraction, then not keeping the safety distance and unsuitable speed.
  • Most common type: on interurban roads, rear-end and multiple collisions; in towns, side and front-side collisions.

3Vulnerable groups

Vulnerable road users are those who, because of how they travel or their age and physical condition, are more exposed and have a much higher risk of serious or fatal injuries in an accident. Since October 2026 the Reglamento General de Circulación defines them: pedestrians (above all people with disabilities, children, older people and people with reduced mobility), cyclists, VMP riders (e-scooters and other personal mobility vehicles) and motorcyclists and moped riders and their passengers. Your course also covers older drivers.

3.1.1 Older drivers

Their main problem is the decline of physical and mental abilities:

Problem
Narrower field of vision, especially at night, and more easily dazzled.
Hearing loss: harder to tell where sounds come from.
Slower response in complex situations (intersections, joining and leaving fast roads): a longer reaction time.
Medicines that may affect driving; less ability to keep attention; less strength to brake and worse handling of the steering wheel.
Remember
  • Be respectful and patient with older people, especially in complex situations.

3.1.2 Pedestrians

Pedestrians have more accidents in towns, but on interurban roads the injuries can be very serious and death is more likely, because of the speeds. In towns the chance of dying when hit is lower, but there are many more pedestrians hit, and more than half of the pedestrians killed die in towns. Their movements are hard to predict: they have a larger zone of uncertainty than other road users.

WhoMost common offences
PedestriansBursting onto the road or crossing incorrectly; standing or walking on the carriageway or shoulder improperly; not using crossings or crossing diagonally; ignoring traffic lights; not respecting priority; getting in or out of a vehicle without watching the traffic.
Drivers, putting pedestrians at riskNot giving way to pedestrians; parking on the pavement or on crossings; not slowing down at crossings; ignoring traffic lights (amber or red).

Older pedestrians have more accidents when they are alone than when they are looking after children, so take extra care with them. Their main problems:

Older pedestrians
Noise stops them hearing vehicles; it is hard for them to judge vehicle speed and see traffic-light colours (especially on very wide roads).
Few crossings in some areas and poor lighting on some roads.
They need more time to cross wide streets; high kerbs and obstacles on pavements (planters, badly parked cars, bollards); getting disoriented in unfamiliar streets.

Children, being shorter, usually take the impact on the head or vital organs. Most child pedestrians are hit when school ends. The main causes:

Children as pedestrians
Hearing: under 7, they cannot tell where the noise of an approaching vehicle comes from.
Limited field of vision: up to 40 % less than adults when walking between parked cars — and drivers find it harder to see them.
Poor attention control: easily distracted, they may run out at any moment.
They confuse “seeing” with “being seen”: if they see a car, they think the driver has seen them too.
They don’t know the traffic rules and cannot judge distances and speeds or recognise real danger.
Avoiding hitting pedestrians: extra attention and slow down…
  • …near a stopped bus, above all a school bus; when leaving a garage (ramps); when a vehicle stops in front (its occupants may get out without looking).
  • …when pedestrians are talking on the phone; on roads near towns and leisure areas, especially in summer; in bad weather (pedestrians take more risks on rainy days).
  • …near crossings, school zones, crowds and people with disabilities; and be careful when reversing.
  • Don’t wave pedestrians across; don’t park on the pavement (it forces them onto the road); don’t modify the outside of the car, especially the front — it is designed to reduce injuries to pedestrians.

Pedestrians walking on the carriageway or shoulder of an interurban road at night or in poor visibility must wear at least one luminous or reflective element visible from 150 m.

3.1.3 Cyclists

Most cyclist accidents come from offences by cyclists and by other drivers (distraction, wrong turns, unsuitable speed, not giving way at intersections…). They happen mostly at weekends, especially in good weather; on conventional roads, above all on straights and at intersections; and mostly as head-on or front-side collisions with another vehicle, followed by rear-end and side impacts.

RuleWhat it says
Where to rideOn the carriageway if there is no bike lane. Where there is one, its use is preferred, and the authority can make it compulsory with signs.
PavementsNot allowed, except children under 12 where the town council allows it, accompanied by an adult on foot.
In townCyclists ride preferably in the centre of the lane. Motor vehicles keep at least 5 m behind a cyclist in the same lane.
Overtaking a cyclistDon’t start or continue if it endangers cyclists coming the other way (even on the shoulder). Leave at least 1.5 m sideways — more with large vehicles, on slopes, in wind or if the cyclist carries a passenger. Out of town, slow to at least 20 km/h below the limit; with more than one lane in your direction, change lane completely.
HelmetCompulsory on interurban roads for every cyclist (the old exceptions were removed in October 2026); on all roads for under-16s and for those who work on a bicycle (couriers, delivery riders).
Being seenOn interurban roads, between sunset and sunrise or in poor visibility: at least one luminous or reflective element visible from 150 m. Those who work on a bicycle wear a high-visibility vest at all times.
Take extra care…
  • …in single-lane town streets limited to 30 km/h or less where signs allow bicycles in both directions: move to your right to let them pass; if that is impossible, vehicles going in the street’s own direction have priority.
  • …near parked vehicles or obstacles (cyclists may swerve suddenly), in housing estates, leisure areas and places with many cyclists, especially in summer and on holidays, and in bad weather or poor visibility (sudden moves and falls).
  • Avoid using the horn near cyclists (it startles them). If you ride, wear a helmet: the most serious injuries are to the head.

3.1.4 Moped and motorcycle riders

What to know
Mopeds and motorcycles are used more and more. They are less visible, less stable and more fragile than other vehicles, and their accidents are easily fatal; not wearing a helmet is one of the main reasons for the high death rate.
Most frequent causes: offences by riders and by others — distractions, not giving way, invading the opposite lane. Most common accident: a head-on or front-side collision when overtaking, especially in towns.
Posture: relaxed and comfortable, not leaning forward more than needed to reach the handlebar; hold it gently but firmly (no tension), arms slightly bent.
An inexperienced passenger makes an accident more likely, especially in bends. With a passenger, braking shifts the centre of gravity (it can unbalance the bike), the rear wheel is harder to lock and the stopping distance is longer.
Riding very slowly in a bend with the handlebar turned: don’t use the front brake (you may fall).
Protective equipment (since 1 October 2026)Rider and passenger
Helmet approved to UNECE R22, fastenedAll roads. Moped users may keep using certified (not approved) helmets until 1 October 2027.
Protective glovesInterurban roads.
Closed footwear covering the whole footAll roads (no sandals or flip-flops).
High-visibility vestA motorcycle must carry one; wear it when you get off and stand on the carriageway or shoulder of an interurban road. Those who work on a motorcycle or moped wear it at all times. Otherwise it is recommended while riding.

Not wearing gloves, closed shoes or (for riders who work on the bike) the vest is a serious offence: 200 €. Your course repeats in this list the 150 m reflective element; in the law that element is for cyclists and VMP riders.

If you ride a moped or motorcycle
  • Be visible (don’t surprise anyone); respect priority at intersections; keep the safety distance and avoid riding alongside other vehicles.
  • Extra care in bad weather or poor visibility (sudden moves and falls). A reflective vest while riding is recommended, not compulsory.
  • If you must use the opposite lane, make sure nothing is coming.
If you fall off
  • Try to slide along the ground as relaxed as possible until you stop.

3.1.5 E-scooters and other personal mobility vehicles (VMP)

E-scooters have become the fashionable urban vehicle — and a particularly vulnerable one in an accident. The rules:

TopicRule
WhoMinimum age 15. Rider only: no passengers.
HelmetCompulsory, approved or certified, properly fastened.
Being seenBetween sunset and sunrise or in poor visibility: a luminous or reflective element visible from 150 m (a reflective vest). Those who work on a VMP wear the vest at all times.
SignalsAlways use your arm to warn of manoeuvres.
Speed and positionMaximum 25 km/h. Preferably in the centre of the lane; motor vehicles keep at least 5 m behind.
EquipmentElectric motor (environmental label CERO, no sticker needed). Two independent brakes (they may share one control). White front light, red rear light, brake light (separate or combined). Reflectors: white front, white or amber sides, red rear. A bell. Lights always on, day and night (the daytime rule applies from 1 October 2027).
Where they may not ridePavements, autopistas and autovías (even inside towns), travesías, interurban roads and urban tunnels — except segregated bike lanes, cycle tracks and paths, and roads closed to motor vehicles, unless signs forbid it.
In townBoth directions allowed in single-lane streets limited to 30 km/h or less, if signed (same as bicycles). Town bylaws set where they may ride (bike lanes, 30 or 20 km/h streets).
General rulesAll the general rules and bans apply: alcohol, drugs, phone… People with reduced mobility riding a VMP at walking pace count as pedestrians.
Other things a VMP needs before it can be ridden
  • Registered in the DGT’s national register of light personal vehicles, with the identification label (in its holder, visible) and the manufacturer’s plate (serial number).
  • A circulation certificate (it meets the technical requirements) and compulsory third-party insurance (since January 2026).
  • VMP sold before 22 January 2024 may be used without the certificate until 21 January 2027; from 22 January 2027 only certified ones. They must still be registered and insured.

3.2 The risk group: young drivers

Young drivers are not vulnerable users, but they are an important risk group because of their high accident rate. Road accidents are the main cause of injury and death for people aged 15 to 29 (almost 35 % of road deaths). The risk rises from 14–15, the age of the first moped riders.

QuestionAnswer
WhenGoing out for fun, with alcohol and several occupants; at night and in the early hours; in and around big cities; commuting; weekends, Christmas and summer.
WhyLack of experience, speeding, breaking rules, alcohol and drugs.
What pushes them to take risksAdvertising that encourages risk; lower perception of risk; accepting unnecessary risks (to prove themselves, competitiveness); not seeing driving as dangerous; showing off in a group (they risk more with friends); overestimating their skill while having less control; thinking that mistakes are always made by others.

4The factors involved

Accidents can be prevented by tackling every risk factor. There are three:

4.1 The human factor

The human factor is the main cause of accidents (70–90 %): most are due to unsuitable behaviour by the driver. You must adapt your behaviour to what driving demands (your state, speed, the road, the weather, traffic density, distractions, rules and signs). Your ability depends on your training and your experience.

The driver’s most frequent causes of accidents
  • Distraction or lack of attention; not keeping the safety distance; excessive or unsuitable speed.
  • Not giving way; wrong turns; illegal overtaking; improper use of the carriageway.

4.1.1 Speed

Speed and the driver
As speed rises, the field of vision narrows — the tunnel effect (efecto túnel): only the centre of the road is seen sharply, and the sides go by too fast to be taken in. Especially dangerous at intersections and with sideways movements.
Less ability to see and analyse what is going on (more serious mistakes): anticipation and reaction get worse. And injuries are more serious.
Driving fast for a long time on wide, good roads makes you feel slower than you really are (take care when entering towns); it raises tension, brings fatigue sooner and makes you more hostile or aggressive.
Remember
  • 90 % of the information needed to drive is visual.
TermMeaning
Reaction timeFrom perceiving a stimulus to responding. Normally between half a second and one second — typically 0.75 s. It grows with age, fatigue and drowsiness, alcohol, drugs and some medicines, mood, illness, stress, and heat or too much heating.
Reaction distanceWhat the vehicle travels during the reaction time. It depends on how fast the driver reacts and on the speed: more speed or a longer reaction time means more distance.
Braking distanceFrom pressing the brake to stopping. It depends on the speed, the vehicle’s mass and load (a passenger on a motorcycle makes it longer), the driving technique, the vehicle’s condition (tyres, brakes, suspension), the road surface and grip, and the weather (rain ×2, snow or ice ×10).
Stopping distance (parada técnica)From seeing the obstacle to stopping: reaction distance + braking distance.

Quick maths: km/h ÷ 3.6 = metres per second. At 90 km/h you cover 25 m every second, so in a typical 0.75 s reaction time the car travels about 19 m before you even touch the brake; at 50 km/h, about 10 m.

To avoid an accident
  • Drive at a speed at which your stopping distance is shorter than the distance to the obstacle.
  • How well a driver responds also depends on the training they have had.

4.1.2 Fatigue and sleep

Fatigue, together with sleep, is one of the main causes of accidents, especially among professional drivers. It harms perception, attention, movement, behaviour and decision-making.

Main effects of fatigue
Muscle stiffness (shifting in the seat, cramps, yawning, back or neck ache); slow, imprecise movements; blurred vision and worse hearing.
Behaviour changes: hostile, irritable, more risks. Less attention and concentration (you lose the sense of speed).
Slower reactions (longer reaction time); fewer steering corrections and more errors; more passive, automatic driving.
Fatigue comes from…Circumstances
The driverLittle experience; driving for long periods without proper breaks (the main cause); bad posture; high speed for a long time; driving sleepy, after alcohol or ill (even a cold); changes in your normal driving habits; stress.
The roadHeavy traffic, jams and hold-ups; a poor road surface; unfamiliar roads; bad weather.
The vehiclePoor condition (suspension, steering, lighting); poor ventilation or high temperature — recommended 20–23 °C, without blowing air at your eyes; an unergonomic seat or interior.

Sleep is one of the biggest dangers. It usually comes with fatigue (each brings on the other) and causes 15–30 % of accidents, usually serious ones. You don’t need to fall asleep to crash: the risks of drowsiness start much earlier, and these accidents happen by day as well as by night.

Why drowsiness raises the risk
Longer reaction time; more distractions (especially on monotonous roads with little traffic); slower decisions with more mistakes.
Slower, less precise, automatic movements; microsleeps — a few seconds asleep without realising it.
Worse perception (tired eyes, blurred vision, more dazzle); behaviour changes (restlessness, hostility, more risk, speeding to arrive sooner).
Tips against drowsiness
Time of day: take care in the early hours (3–5 h) and the early afternoon (14–16 h). Avoid driving when you would normally be asleep; extra care with shift work.
Sleep quality and quantity: sleeping badly is as dangerous as sleeping too little; 7–9 hours of deep sleep is right.
Monotony: driving at night on an empty motorway brings on sleep. Heavy meals sedate; high temperatures cause sleepiness.
Sedatives and stimulants: alcohol and medicines bring on sleep; tea or coffee have a rebound effect — sleep comes suddenly when they wear off.
Individual differences and sleep disorders: insomnia can bring daytime sleepiness; narcolepsy legally prevents getting a licence.
Reducing the risk from fatigue or sleep
  • Watch for the first signs of tiredness or sleep; if they appear, the best thing is to stop and rest in a suitable place.
  • Stop at least every 2 hours or 200 km (more often if tired), for 20–30 minutes: stretch your legs, get some air and, if needed, sleep.

Rumble strips (guías sonoras longitudinales fresadas, GSLF) are bands milled into the asphalt that warn the driver, by noise and vibration, of an unintended lane departure. They give extra time to correct the path before leaving the road or crossing into oncoming traffic, and add safety without big changes to the road.

4.1.3 Illness and medicines

Illness and medicines can affect the basic abilities needed to drive safely (especially mental illness and neurological disorders). Drivers with a chronic illness should: know the illness and the side effects of their medicines; recognise the first symptoms of a crisis and know what to do; avoid what triggers a crisis; never drink alcohol while taking medicines; and ask their doctor when in doubt.

ConditionEffects on drivingAdvice
AllergiesCold-like symptoms: misjudged distances, less concentration, especially in a sneezing fit. Antihistamines can cause strong drowsiness, especially first-generation ones; newer ones (third generation) are safer, but never with alcohol or drugs.Keep the windows closed; air conditioning not too strong; clean interior and vents; no alcohol when on medication; no very long trips; sunglasses; avoid driving at dawn and in damp areas; don’t self-medicate.
StressMore aggression, hostility and competitiveness; more reckless, more risk accepted; tendency to ignore signs and rules; slower decisions, more errors; more distractions; fatigue sooner.Seek specialist help; don’t drive unless strictly necessary (especially in the worst phase, or if on medication).
DepressionMore distractions (absorbed in thoughts); you miss information from the surroundings; more sensitive to drowsiness and fatigue; irritability and anxiety; psychotropic drugs can seriously impair driving. The law forbids driving under the effects of certain psychotropics (antidepressants, anxiolytics, sedatives, hypnotics, antipsychotics).See a specialist before driving; don’t self-medicate or take alcohol or other drugs; avoid driving in the most acute phase; avoid night, monotonous or very long drives.
Medicines: not everyone reacts the same
Ask your doctor or pharmacist about the risks; follow the doses and times prescribed; never self-medicate or mix with alcohol.
Read the leaflet to see whether it affects driving — alternative or natural remedies can have negative effects too.
Try not to drive, or be very careful, at the start of any treatment; don’t mix medicines (unless the doctor says so); careful with coffee and other substances that change their effect.
PictogramWhat it means
“Driving: see the leaflet” (Conducción: ver prospecto). It appears on the box of some medicines and warns — it does not forbid — that you should read the leaflet, which describes all the side effects that can affect a driver.

4.1.4 Heat

Effects of heat on the driverHow to avoid the risk
Longer reaction time; more mistakes; more fatigue, sleepiness and distraction; more hostility and aggression towards others.More stops (20–30 min every 2 h or 200 km); avoid parking in the sun; drink water or juice, avoid hot, heavy meals and take care after eating; light, pale clothes and good sunglasses; air conditioning at 20–23 °C.

4.1.5 Distractions

Distractions are the risk factor that has grown the most in the last decade — behind one in three fatal accidents. Especially among young drivers (18–25) and over-70s; when the driver has company (talking, arguing, noisy children); in summer, at weekends and on leisure trips; and on the open road, especially autopistas and autovías (monotony). To drive safely, give all your attention to driving.

Using the mobile phone — held in the hand or even hands-free
Attention drops. The most dangerous moments: answering, dialling or texting, talking, and hanging up or putting the phone down.
More offences: after a minute and a half, 40 % of signs go unnoticed. Distances are misjudged (the safety distance shrinks).
Worse speed control: sudden changes; after a minute and a half the average speed drops 12 %.
Swerving and poor handling — the most frequent phone accident is running off the road; disorientation and bad decisions. It is like driving with 1 g/l of alcohol in the blood.
Phone rules
  • Using the phone by hand while driving is prohibited — even when stopped at traffic lights. Holding it in your hand: 6 points and 200 €.
  • With hands-free, tell the caller you are driving and don’t talk for more than a minute. Better still, don’t use it: stop somewhere safe. Take care also because a ringing phone, like any noise, can startle you.
Sat-navs (GPS)
Plan the trip before setting off and programme speed limits if possible (choose the safest route); follow the voice instructions rather than the screen.
Watch the signs, the road and the traffic: even if the sat-nav suggests a route, your own judgement always comes first.
A portable unit needs a proper mount (so it can’t fall), placed where it doesn’t block your view or make you look away — and never near the airbag; route the cables away from the wheel and gear lever. Your main speed reference is the speedometer.
Smoking
Lighting up and smoking takes one hand off the controls and distracts; smokers tend to rate traffic situations as less dangerous and take more risks.
The carbon monoxide (CO) in smoke lowers attention; smoke causes vision problems; and smoking brings medical problems, mainly cardiovascular.
Smoking at the wheel
  • It is recommended not to smoke while driving, but it is not prohibited. Throwing a cigarette end out of the window is: it can start a fire (6 points, Topic 9).

4.1.6 Alcohol

Alcohol makes an accident more likely and its injuries more serious. It is a depressant of the central nervous system, although at first it has a euphoric phase.

What alcohol changesHow
BehaviourFalse sense of safety and control; less prudent; more offences; impulsive and aggressive responses.
PerceptionPerceives worse, misjudges distances, more sensitive to dazzle, and may suffer tunnel vision.
AttentionMore distractions.
Psychomotor skillsLess precision and coordination.

The blood alcohol level (tasa de alcoholemia) is the amount of alcohol in the blood. The only truly safe level is 0.0 g/l: below the legal limit you can still crash because of alcohol.

DriverExhaled airBlood
General (after the first 2 years of the licence), including cyclists and VMP riders0.25 mg/l0.5 g/l
Any driver in the first two years of their licence; professional drivers0.15 mg/l0.3 g/l
Drivers under 18 (any vehicle, bicycles and mopeds included)0.0 mg/l0.0 g/l
You can’t fool the breathalyser
  • There are no tricks: exercise, chewing gum or sweets, coffee, oil, smoking, mouth sprays, a short nap or lots of water — none of them works.
Effects depend onHow
The driverWeight (more effect on slim people); sex (more effect on women); age (more on under-18s and over-65s); circumstances (fatigue, sleep, stress, illness); experience — the effects are greater on inexperienced drivers, which is why their limit is lower.
How it is drunkQuantity — the most important factor. Time: in the blood after 5 minutes, highest level after 30–90 minutes, then disappears very slowly over several hours. Speed: drinking fast raises it more. Time of day: eliminated more slowly while asleep. Type: fermented drinks (beer, wine) are absorbed more slowly than distilled ones (gin, rum, whisky, vodka); fizzy or hot drinks act faster. Empty stomach: alcohol passes into the blood faster (higher level).
Remember
  • The effects of alcohol are not always the same: two people who drink the same need not reach the same level.

4.1.7 Drugs

Driving on public roads is prohibited for any driver — cyclists and VMP riders included — with drugs in their body (narcotics, psychotropics, stimulants, or medicines and similar substances that alter the physical or mental state). The exception is substances taken on prescription for treatment, as long as they don’t affect driving. Many of the most serious accidents are linked to drugs, and mixed with alcohol their effects become unpredictable.

DrugEffects on the driver
CannabisDistorted perception of surroundings, time and space; loss of concentration; longer reaction time; drowsiness.
CocaineAggressive, impulsive, competitive behaviour; overestimating your abilities; distorted perception; less concentration.
Ecstasy (MDMA)Optical illusions and blurred vision; more sensitive to dazzle; depression and anxiety; less concentration; physical and mental exhaustion when it wears off (flashbacks hours later).
LSDStrong distortions of reality and hallucinations; emotional changes (aggression, anxiety, panic); effects can last 10–12 hours (flashbacks possible).
AmphetaminesImpulsive and violent behaviour; overestimating abilities (false security); repetitive movements; they hide fatigue and sleepiness — and sleep comes back with a rebound effect.

4.1.8 Alcohol, drugs and the law

StepRule
Who can be testedTraffic agents can test for alcohol or drugs: any road user directly involved as possibly responsible in an accident, or who has committed an offence; and any driver (cyclists and VMP included) involved in an accident, with obvious symptoms, who has committed an offence or who is simply stopped at a preventive check.
Type of testAlcohol: exhaled air, with approved breathalysers (etilómetros). Drugs: a saliva test with an approved device, then a lab analysis. At the person’s request or by court order, contrast tests can be done — preferably a blood test, or urine or similar.
If the result is over the limit (or there are obvious symptoms, even below it)The agent explains: a second, similar test follows, at least 10 minutes after the first (the person, companions or witnesses may check the time); you may make any statements; and you have the right to a contrast analysis (blood, urine or other), paid in advance by you — charged to you if positive, refunded if negative.
Immobilising the vehicleIf the result is positive (unless another properly licensed person can drive), or if the driver refuses the tests. It ends when the cause disappears (unless a court orders otherwise) or another driver takes over. The costs of immobilising, towing and storage are paid by the driver or whoever is legally responsible.
ResultFinePoints
Alcohol over the limit, up to twice it (0.25–0.50 mg/l; new and professional drivers 0.15–0.30)500 €4
Alcohol over twice the limit (over 0.50 mg/l; new and professional drivers over 0.30)1,000 €6
Drugs in the body1,000 €6

In serious cases it becomes a crime and can mean prison: over 0.60 mg/l in air (1.2 g/l in blood), driving under the influence of drugs, or refusing the tests (Topic 9).

4.2 The vehicle factor

Modern vehicles have safety devices that make an accident less likely or less serious, but cannot prevent it completely; some even have automated driving. The driver’s role is essential for them to work: maintain the vehicle properly even if it is little used, especially near the beach (salt corrosion). The vehicle factor is involved in 4–13 % of accidents.

The vehicle’s most frequent causes of accidents
  • Failure of the tyres (the most frequent), the brakes, the lights or the steering; too much load or badly spread load.

4.2.1 The driving position

Before starting the engine, adjust…So that…
The seatYou can press the pedals all the way down without moving your body forward, with your legs slightly bent.
The backrest and the steering wheelBoth hands reach the top of the wheel without your back leaving the backrest; in the normal position your arms are slightly bent.
Seat and wheel heightYou see the road over the wheel.
Then…Head restraint, mirrors and seat belt.
The most frequent wrong settings
  • Too close to the wheel: fatigue, less mobility (forced, slower movements) and danger from the airbag.
  • Too far from the wheel: you can’t act quickly and effectively, and the passive safety devices don’t work properly.

4.2.2 The controls

Car controlUse
Steering wheel (hands)Steers the front wheels. Both hands on the outside, firm but not tense, at “ten to two” or “quarter to three”. Don’t cross your hands to turn.
Gear lever (hand)Choose the right gear: low gears give more force but less speed; high gears, less force but more speed.
Handbrake (hand)Keeps the vehicle immobilised.
Clutch (left foot)Released (engaged): the gearbox receives the engine’s turn and, in gear, sends it to the driving wheels. Pressed (disengaged): it stops receiving it, so you can change gear.
Service brake (right foot)Slows down or stops the vehicle safely and smoothly.
Accelerator (right foot)Raises the engine speed (rpm, revolutions per minute).

4.2.3 Active safety: tyres

Active safety tries to prevent an accident from happening. Its main elements: wheels, brakes, suspension, steering and lights. The wheels are the only part touching the ground, so they need the most attention: they are the main cause of accidents from mechanical failure. A wheel is the rim, the tyre and, in some, an inner tube.

Part of the tyreWhat it is
TreadThe part in contact with the ground; its grooves give grip and clear the water on the road.
ShouldersJoin the tread and the sidewall.
CarcassInternal structure that bears the weight and the pressure.
BeadsJoin the tyre to the rim.
SidewallsThe sides of the tyre.
MarkingMeaning
225Nominal width in millimetres.
70Profile: the sidewall height is 70 % of the width.
RRadial structure.
16Rim diameter in inches.
110Load index: maximum load per tyre (110 = 1,060 kg).
SSpeed symbol: maximum speed (S = 180 km/h).
TUBELESSTyre without an inner tube.
DOT 3221Manufacturing date: week 32 of 2021.
M+S (M&S, MS)Tyres with better grip in mud (M) and snow (S).
Changing load index or speed code
  • You may fit tyres whose load index and speed code are equal to or higher than the manufacturer’s. Fitting lower ones is prohibited.
Type of tyreFeature
TubelessThe air is held between the rim and the tyre; safer in a puncture — it loses air slowly.
With inner tubeThe air is in a tube inside; less safe.
RadialThe carcass has rubberised cords and wires laid out like radii.
The EU tyre label
Gives buyers fuller information to compare tyres before buying.
Top: a QR code (more information in the EU product database), brand or trade name, tyre type identifier, size with load and speed indexes, class, and the classes for fuel efficiency and wet grip (A to E).
Bottom: the external rolling noise (decibels and class) and two pictograms showing whether its grip meets the standards for snow (3PMSF) and ice.
Tyre pressure
Check it regularly — about every 15 days — with cold tyres and a gauge in good condition. If you check with hot tyres, don’t let air out: the manufacturer allows for the rise.
Use the pressure recommended by the manufacturer (by load and type of road). The spare wheel goes at the highest recommended pressure. Don’t change the pressure between winter and summer.
Wrong pressureConsequences
Too lowSidewalls deform and overheat; wear on the edges (risk of a blow-out); less grip (aquaplaning); more fuel (more rolling resistance).
Too highSmaller contact area (less grip); wear in the centre of the tread; bumps are not absorbed and the suspension suffers.
Unequal on the same axle (the most dangerous)The car pulls to one side on a straight road; less stability; uneven braking.
Changing tyres
Change them when the tread depth reaches 1.6 mm (2 mm recommended), when they have cuts, cracks or bulges, or when they have expired (recommended after 5 years from manufacture).
New tyres should be the same on all wheels, or at least the same on each axle.
Wider tyres use more fuel and reduce safety (they harm the brakes, suspension and steering).
Changing a wheel, step by step
1. Find a suitable place and immobilise the vehicle properly.
2. Signal it: hazard lights + the V-16 warning light. Put the vest on before getting out.
3. Chock the vehicle and place the jack — never get under a car held up by the jack.
4. Loosen the nuts before lifting the car with the jack.
5. Change the wheel and tighten the nuts with the car on the ground.
6. Check the nuts after 20–30 km (again after 150–250 km is recommended). With a temporary spare, keep to its limits (for example 80 km/h and 200 km).
A blow-out
  • Stay calm, hold the wheel firmly and correct any swerve (keep your line).
  • Don’t take your foot off the accelerator suddenly, and brake as little as possible, very gently.
Other tyre careCauses of faster wear
Inspect the tyres and remove stones stuck in the grooves; put the tyres in best condition on the rear axle; balance the wheels at a workshop if the steering wheel vibrates at certain speeds (after hitting kerbs…).Wrong pressure; aggressive driving; high speed and too much load; heat (more in summer); unbalanced wheels; worn brakes or shock absorbers; the road surface and chains (take them off when not needed).

4.2.3 Active safety: brakes

Brakes slow the vehicle down, stop it or keep it still. How well it brakes depends on the pressure on the pedal, the vehicle’s condition (brakes, tyres, suspension), the load, the speed and the road.

Servo brake
  • It multiplies the force the driver applies, so braking takes less effort — but it only works with the engine running. With the engine off you must press much harder.
Braking systemWhat it does
Service brake (foot brake)Slows and stops the vehicle; acts on all the wheels.
Emergency brake (freno de socorro)The last part of the foot brake’s travel; stops the vehicle if the service brake fails. Acts on at least one wheel on each side.
Parking brake (handbrake)Keeps the vehicle still, even with nobody in it. Usually acts on the rear wheels (by hand or electric).
Engine brakeUsing the engine to slow down: lift off the accelerator or shift down (especially on long downhill stretches).
Why use the engine brake
  • You don’t surprise drivers behind with sudden stops (fewer rear-end crashes); less brake wear and no fading; less fuel and pollution (fuel use drops to zero).
Braking normally
Brake as early as possible (use the engine brake; avoid sudden braking after checking it is safe); brake smoothly and progressively; don’t overuse the brakes.
Adapt braking to the surface and its grip (especially with low grip and without ABS).
On long descents, use the engine brake and low gears (don’t ride the clutch). Overusing the brakes causes fading — they lose effect as they overheat. An overloaded vehicle brakes worse.
Emergency braking
  • 1. Press the brake as hard as you can. Without ABS: if the wheels lock, ease off and press hard again. With ABS: keep pressing hard even if the pedal vibrates.
  • 2. Press the clutch just before the vehicle stops.
SystemWhat it does
ABS (anti-lock braking)Prevents the wheels from locking, adapts braking to the grip and lets you keep steering.
BAS (brake assist)Detects emergency braking and raises the braking pressure on all wheels, without locking them.
If the brakes fail
1. Pump the pedal (press and release). If you think they have overheated, release the pedal and let them cool.
2. Move to the right or onto the shoulder and shift down (engine brake).
3. Use the handbrake gently and progressively.
4. Look for an emergency escape lane (lecho de frenado), an uphill slope, or scrape along the side to slow down by friction.
SymptomLikely causeWhat to do
You must press harder than usual (a metallic noise if very worn)Worn pads or shoesWorkshop: replace them
Soft, spongy pedalAir in the hydraulic circuitWorkshop: bleed the system
Pedal goes almost to the floorLoss of brake fluidWorkshop: fix the leak and refill between min and max
Car pulls to one side when brakingDifferent pressures on the same axle, uneven brake wear, bad adjustment or blocked brake hosesCheck the tyre pressure; if that doesn’t fix it, workshop
Less effect after a puddle or a car washToo much moisturePress the brakes several times to dry them by friction

To maintain the brakes, check the brake fluid level (between the min and max marks), replace the fluid, keep the hoses clean (no cracks or leaks) and change pads and discs as the manufacturer says. Bad brakes are the first reason vehicles fail the ITV.

Brake typeHow it works
Disc brakeThe disc turns with the wheel; the pads squeeze it. The most used: shorter braking distance, less risk of locking, better cooled (less fading).
Drum brakeThe drum turns with the wheel; the shoes expand against it.

4.2.3 Active safety: suspension, steering, lights and other systems

The suspension joins the wheels to the rest of the vehicle, absorbs bumps and controls body roll so it doesn’t affect stability. Smart suspension lets you choose: hard for bends or fast driving (you feel the bumps more), soft for good roads and motorways (more comfortable). The steering lets the driver direct the vehicle: power steering reduces the effort; speed-sensitive power steering stiffens with speed for better control.

SymptomLikely causeSolution
Bounces too much over bumpsWorn shock absorbers or tyres over-inflatedCheck pressures or replace the shock absorbers
Leans too much (braking, bends)Worn shock absorbers or tyres under-inflatedCheck pressures or replace the shock absorbers
Bounces when braking and needs more distance to stopWorn shock absorbersReplace them
Heavy steeringTyres under-inflated or wrong alignmentCheck pressures or workshop
Steering has play (the wheel doesn’t respond at once)A worn partWorkshop
Pulls to one side when you let go of the wheelDifferent pressures on the same axle or wrong alignmentCheck pressures or workshop

For the steering, check the power-steering fluid level (between min and max), keep it aligned and avoid hitting kerbs and potholes.

Lights: to see, be seen and signalWhat to know
Xenon and bi-xenonClose to daylight; a wider lit area and less eye strain.
LEDLights up to three times further than xenon, with a whiter light.
Daytime running lightsMake the vehicle more visible in all circumstances.
Adaptive lightsTurn with the steering, lighting bends and intersections.
MaintenanceCheck that they work and are clean (dirt or damage can deflect the beam and dazzle); check the fuses if a light fails. Check the aim, especially after loading or unloading: aimed too low, you see obstacles later; too high, it lights the road worse and dazzles others.
Other active-safety systemsWhat it does
ESP (electronic stability control)Corrects a skid before it happens, braking individual wheels and adjusting the engine’s power.
Traction controlDetects a driving wheel spinning faster than it should (slippery ground, bends) and cuts engine power and/or brakes.
Speed limiter / cruise controlHelps keep the chosen speed: some stop you exceeding a set speed; others hold it without touching the pedals; some also keep the distance to the vehicle ahead.

4.2.4 Passive safety

Passive safety reduces the consequences of an accident: it prevents or reduces injuries. Main elements: chassis and body, glass, seat belts, child restraints, airbags, head restraints and motorcyclists’ equipment.

Body and chassis
They carry every part of the car and protect the occupants by absorbing as much of the crash energy as possible.
The central cell (chassis and passenger compartment) stays rigid; the rest (body) deforms progressively and absorbs the impact — a programmed deformation (crumple zones).
Don’t modify the bodywork: a pedestrian who is hit could be hurt more. A strong body does not replace seat belts, head restraints or airbags — they complement each other.
GlassWhen it breaksUsually used in
LaminatedCracks into long pieces that stay joined: you can still see, and it doesn’t injure the occupants.The windscreen
TemperedBreaks into small pieces that block the view and can come loose and hurt the occupants.Rear and side windows

To avoid a windscreen broken by flying gravel, keep more distance from the vehicle ahead.

The seat belt holds the body in a crash or rollover, so occupants don’t hit the inside or get thrown out. It almost halves the risk of dying, especially together with the airbag — they complement each other, neither replaces the other. Some belts have a load limiter that eases the pressure on chest and pelvis when the force is very high.

After a serious crash
  • It is recommended to replace the seat belt: the webbing and the pyrotechnic pretensioners (they fire when the impact is detected) may have lost their effect, and the anchorages may be damaged.
Wearing the belt correctly
In perfect condition, properly anchored, fastened and snug (neither loose nor too tight).
Diagonal strap: over the collarbone (between shoulder and neck), across the middle of the chest. Lap strap: over the hip bones (pelvis) and below the belly — badly placed, it can cause serious injuries.
Sit upright (backrest not too reclined); avoid bulky clothes (coats, thick jumpers); belt clips are prohibited (they slacken it); don’t sit on cushions or towels — the submarining effect: in a crash the body slides under the lap strap.

Children (under 18) 135 cm tall or less must use an approved child restraint suited to their size and weight (a child seat), following the maker’s instructions. Never carry them in your arms.

Child restraints: recommendations
The safest position is generally facing backwards — keep the child rear-facing as long as possible. The rear centre seat is the safest (least affected by side impacts).
ISOFIX: simpler, correct and firm fitting. Lets the child travel rear-facing at least until 15 months or 83 cm (some up to 105 cm); some rotate 360° to make it easier to seat the child.
i-Size: the newest seats, chosen by the child’s height; they add a top tether or a support leg, and work together with ISOFIX.
Never…
  • …fit a rear-facing child seat on a front seat with an airbag unless the airbag has been switched off.

An airbag is a bag that inflates automatically in a violent deceleration, so occupants don’t hit the wheel, windscreen or windows. There are front, side, knee and curtain airbags, and even pedestrian airbags (sensors in the front bumper fire a bag under the bonnet, by the windscreen); some motorcycles have them too.

Airbag recommendations
Sit about 25 cm from the airbag — never less than 10 cm: it inflates at about 300 km/h.
Always with the seat belt (they complement each other). Proper posture — no feet on the dashboard.
Switch off the passenger airbag for a rear-facing child seat. No objects (sat-nav or others) near an airbag.

The head restraint prevents or reduces neck injuries (whiplash, latigazo cervical) from the sudden movement of the head backwards (hyperextension) and then forwards (hyperflexion), above all in rear-end crashes. Use one in every seat (compulsory in the front seats) and adjust it.

There are passive and active head restraints; active ones move to the head automatically in a crash and are more effective. Note: your course writes the two neck movements the other way round — bending back is hyperextension, bending forward is hyperflexion.

HelmetProtection
Full-face (integral)Covers the whole head and face — the recommended one.
ModularThe lower front (chin bar) lifts up.
Open-face (jet)Does not cover the chin.

The helmet absorbs much of the impact energy, greatly reducing fatal injuries, and protects head and face from abrasion on the road. Not wearing one is the main cause of death in motorcycle and moped accidents. It is compulsory for rider and passenger.

Choosing a helmet
Approved to UNECE Regulation 22 (label inside): it has passed the safety tests. Integral type recommended; the right size (snug); strong material.
Straps and fasteners properly done up so it can’t fly off; light, bright, reflective colours (more visible).
Visor in perfect condition, preferably anti-fog (glasses if the helmet has no visor); good ventilation (less fogging).
Replace the helmet
  • Replace (throw away) the helmet after an accident or any hard knock.
Rider’s equipmentWhat to know
Suit or jacketPreferably leather or another abrasion-resistant material, with protection (back, knees, elbows); bright or reflective colours.
Closed footwearCovers the whole foot; compulsory on all roads since October 2026. High boots, snug, with a heel are best; no sandals or flip-flops.
GlovesCompulsory on interurban roads. They protect from cold, keep your hands sensitive for good control and protect them in a fall.
Reflective vestRecommended while riding; part of the motorcycle’s compulsory equipment, worn when you get off onto the carriageway or shoulder of an interurban road.

4.2.5 Driver-assistance systems (ADAS)

ADAS (Advanced Driver Assistance Systems; sistemas avanzados de asistencia a la conducción) are systems that help the driver, making driving and decisions safer for them and for others. In general they collect information through cameras and sensors and warn the driver or even act on the controls. Most can be switched off by the driver, temporarily or permanently.

Two warnings
  • The driver keeps an active role: however many systems the car has, keep full attention and control and don’t take more risks trusting that they will act for you.
  • In some cars, ADAS lose their calibration when the battery is disconnected (it depends on the make and model), as happens with the steering-angle sensors.
Compulsory in new cars
  • Under EU Regulation 2019/2144, every new vehicle registered since 6 July 2024 must have a set of ADAS — for cars, among others: ISA, drowsiness warning, emergency braking (AEB), lane keeping, reversing detection, tyre-pressure monitoring, the emergency stop signal and the event data recorder. Pedestrian and cyclist AEB is required in new cars registered from 6 July 2026.
Main ADASWhat it does
ISA — intelligent speed assistanceCombines adaptive cruise control and traffic-sign recognition: a camera behind the rear-view mirror reads the signs and the system keeps a suitable speed by reducing engine revs — it never brakes. Switched on or off by the driver.
ACC — adaptive cruise controlCruise control keeps a set speed and switches off when you brake; the adaptive version also keeps the safety distance to the vehicle ahead automatically.
Emergency braking warning (your course: EBD)In hard braking the brake lights flash quickly to warn those behind (in EU rules, the emergency stop signal). Your course also describes another system with the same initials: electronic brake-force distribution, which shares the braking force between the wheels.
AEB / AEBS — automatic emergency brakingA front radar detects imminent danger; if the driver ignores the warnings (sound and light), the car brakes by itself to avoid or reduce the collision. In town and out of town.
LDW — lane departure warning (and LKA / ELKS)Cameras read the lane lines and warn (sound, light or vibration in the wheel or seat) of an unintended drift. It stays off if you signal or steer evasively; usually active from 60–80 km/h. Lane keeping (LKA / ELKS) goes further: it corrects the steering or brakes the wheels on the other side.
RCTA — rear cross-traffic alertWhen reversing out of a space, warns of people, objects or vehicles crossing behind (up to 30 m); some brake by themselves below 15 km/h. Still check the mirrors and look directly.
Rear camera and 360° systemShow the area behind or a virtual bird’s-eye view, with guide lines or red arrows marking danger. They switch on when you engage reverse or press a button.
Parking assistUltrasonic sensors find a big enough space; the system steers (sometimes brakes) to park — and helps you leave.
DDAW / DDR-ADR — drowsiness and distraction warningChecks whether the driver is alert and taking part (some watch eyes and head) and advises stopping to rest.
Alcolock interfaceA standard connection to fit a breathalyser that stops the engine starting if the driver is over the limit. Your course: compulsory in professional and public-transport vehicles.
Hill holder, Start-Stop, head-up displayHill holder: stops the car rolling back when you lift off the brake on a slope. Start-Stop: stops the engine at idle and restarts it when you press the clutch (less fuel and emissions). HUD: projects data into your line of sight.
Automatic lights and wipersA sensor detects darkness or rain. Also automatic high beam, cornering lights and adaptive lighting (shapes the beam so others are not dazzled).
Seat-belt reminder, TPM, sign recognition, night visionBelt warning for front and rear seats; tyre-pressure monitoring while driving; a camera reads speed-limit and no-overtaking signs (gives priority to the last one; falls back on map data); infrared images of pedestrians or animals beyond the headlights.
EDR — event data recorder (“black box”)Records key data just before, during and after a collision (speed, braking, position, safety systems, eCall). It cannot be switched off.
ADAS aftermarket
  • A car already registered without ADAS can have one fitted by an ADAS aftermarket maker, as long as it is a warning system that does not act on the car’s driving controls.
Other ADASWhat it does
FCW — forward collision warningDetects pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles, moving or still; warns if you are too close and in a critical moment can help stop the car.
BSM — blind-spot monitorWarns (sound, a light near the door mirror, or vibration) of vehicles coming up in the next lanes; some act on steering or brakes, but the driver stays in full control.
Exit warningRear sensors warn occupants of cyclists or vehicles coming from behind before they open a door.
eCallWhen the airbags go off it calls 112 automatically (or by pressing SOS); operators answer in the caller’s language anywhere in Europe. It cuts response time.
Evasive steering assistFrom 30 km/h, works out an escape path and helps the steering — only while the driver is steering.
Turn assistTurning left with the indicator on, up to 10 km/h, it brakes if an oncoming vehicle is coming.
Pre-crash safety, adaptive suspension and steering, predictive efficiencyBefore an unavoidable crash (even from behind): tightens the belts, closes the windows, moves the seats. Adapts suspension and steering (sport or comfort). Uses the route to slow down or change gear efficiently.

ADAS in the driving test. The DGT’s instruction COND 2024/12 lists the systems allowed in the practical test. Any system not listed must be switched off. Your course prints the same heading over both lists; in the instruction the second group is “allowed, and graded”: if one of those systems warns or steps in, the examiner judges what happened.

GroupSystems
Allowed, no effect on the gradeStart-Stop; hill holder; reversing detection (REV); rear camera, 360° camera and parking sensors (not full self-parking, which is not allowed); emergency braking warning; speed limiter (SLI); event data recorder (EDR); sign recognition (TSR, passive only); ISA with its automatic speed control (SCF) switched off — your course says the speed-limit warning (SLWF) too.
Allowed, and graded if they actTyre-pressure monitoring (TPM); automatic lights and wipers (if they don’t switch on when needed, you must do it); AEB and pedestrian/cyclist AEB (an intervention counts like the instructor stepping in); pedestrian and cyclist collision warning (VIS-DET); RCTA; drowsiness and distraction warnings (DDR-DAD, DDR-ADR); blind-spot information (BSIS); lane keeping (LKA); lane departure warning (LDW).

4.3 The road and its surroundings

So that driving doesn’t become dangerous, adapt the way you drive to the road (surface, layout…) and to the weather (rain, snow, fog…). The road factor is involved in 10–35 % of accidents.

GripDepends on the road’s condition, the type of surface and the vehicle’s condition
Good gripAsphalt, rigid and rough surfaces (not shiny), especially dry and clean.
Poor gripSmooth surfaces or cobbles; a wet road, gravel, leaves, snow, or some very slippery road markings.
Bicycles, mopeds and motorcycles
  • In bad weather, watch for road markings — they are very slippery. Slow down before reaching them, keep the vehicle upright while crossing and don’t brake on them.
Forces in a bendWhat it does
Centrifugal forceThe most dangerous: it pushes the vehicle to the outside of the bend, along a straight line. It grows with a tighter bend (smaller radius), more speed and more weight (vehicle and load). Speed counts most: double the speed, four times the force.
Centripetal forceThe result of what the driver does to take the bend (turning the wheel, driving technique).

A skid happens when the wheels lose grip and the vehicle slides sideways, especially in bends. Causes: sudden use of the accelerator, brake or steering; too much speed together with a vehicle in poor condition (worn or under-inflated tyres, damaged suspension, worn brakes) or a slippery surface.

SkidWhat to do
Caused by too much brakingRelease the brake.
Front axle slidesStraighten the steering.
Rear axle slidesTurn the wheel towards the same side as the skid.
Avoiding skids
  • Moderate your speed, increase the safety distance (to avoid surprises) and use the accelerator, brake and steering smoothly.

4.3.2 Weather

WeatherTo see and be seenFor grip
Rain — most dangerous with the first dropsCompulsory lights (high beams can dazzle off the water); wipers and demister; extra care overtaking or following large vehicles (more distance).Brake early and gently (braking distance can double); watch dips and flooding; wet brakes lose effect — dry them with short presses; slow down (aquaplaning). Small puddles: between the wheels or with all of them, slowly if only one side; large puddles: very slowly, in first gear if needed.
Snow — most dangerous with the first flakes and when it hardensClear snow off all the glass before setting off; compulsory lights; wipers (stop to clear them if needed); sunglasses by day (glare from the snow).Move off gently, in second gear, wheels straight; smooth driving, no braking or sudden moves; more distance, low speed, the highest gear possible. Uphill: long gears, slow and steady; downhill: low gears (engine brake). Thick snow: drive in other vehicles’ ruts; thin snow: where there are no ruts. Chains (at least on the driving wheels) or snow tyres. On hard snow or ice: don’t brake or accelerate.
Ice — the most dangerous: grip almost nil, stopping distance ×10Clear the ice off the glass before setting off (scraper, heating aimed at it, rear-window heater).Chains (driving wheels) or special tyres (winter, snow or studded); smooth driving — no sudden acceleration, braking or steering; the highest gear possible.
Fog — also dust clouds and smokeCompulsory lights; follow the road markings and other vehicles’ lights; keep the car ventilated and the demister on.Slow down to match the visibility; more distance (pile-ups); avoid overtaking; stop somewhere safe if visibility is almost nil.
Aquaplaning and ice
  • Aquaplaning: at too high a speed the tread can’t clear the water and the tyre floats on it — the car ignores the steering and brakes. Worst with worn tyres and on two-wheelers.
  • Ice is common when it is near or below 0 °C, at night or at dawn, and in damp, shady places (bridges, underpasses, ditches, tree-lined stretches) and dips.
  • If snow is forecast: a full tank, warm clothes (even blankets), water and food, a torch, and a charged phone with charger.
Snow rules
  • On autopistas and autovías, when snow makes driving difficult, overtaking is prohibited and you must use the right-hand lane (also the next one where there are three or more lanes), leaving the left lanes free for emergency vehicles and snowploughs.
  • Traffic authorities and agents can make chains compulsory — a snow spray does not count. If you don’t comply, you are fined and the vehicle is immobilised.

Wind is dangerous when it blows from the side or in gusts. The most affected: bicycles, mopeds, motorcycles and bulky vehicles (vans, lorries, trailers). Slow down, hold the wheel firmly turned slightly into the wind, and watch for the screen effect (buildings, tunnels, bulky vehicles that suddenly block the wind).

Sun
The sun can dazzle. Choose a good departure time (avoid sunrise and sunset); wear sunglasses — but never at night or in tunnels; use the sun visor; keep the windows clean.

5Classic exam traps

Read twice
  • More accidents in towns, more deaths on interurban roads. Most interurban accidents: straight roads with good visibility, running off the road.
  • Young drivers are a risk group, not vulnerable users. Older pedestrians have more accidents alone than with children.
  • Behind a cyclist in town: 5 m. Overtaking: 1.5 m and, out of town, 20 km/h below the limit. Children under 12 on the pavement only with an adult on foot and if the town allows it.
  • VMP: 15 years, helmet, 25 km/h, no passenger, never on pavements, interurban roads, travesías or autovías.
  • Reaction time 0.75 s; stopping distance = reaction + braking. Rain ×2, ice ×10 (braking distance).
  • You can crash from drowsiness without falling asleep. Coffee has a rebound effect.
  • The medicine pictogram warns, it does not forbid. Smoking while driving is not prohibited.
  • Phone: the most dangerous moments are answering, dialling, talking and hanging up; the most frequent accident is running off the road. Even at a red light, no hands.
  • Alcohol: fermented drinks absorb more slowly than distilled; an empty stomach and fizzy drinks speed it up; quantity matters most. Under-18 drivers: 0.0.
  • Second breath test: at least 10 minutes later. Contrast blood test: you pay first, refunded if negative.
  • Clutch released = engaged. Motorcycle: right hand throttle and front brake, left foot gears.
  • Pressure: check cold, every 15 days; spare at the highest pressure; unequal on one axle is the most dangerous. Tread 1.6 mm. Best tyres on the rear axle.
  • Emergency braking with ABS: keep pressing hard even if the pedal vibrates. Servo brake works only with the engine running.
  • Rear-axle skid: steer towards the skid. Front-axle skid: straighten.
  • Thick snow: in the ruts; thin snow: where there are none. Snow on motorways: no overtaking, right-hand lane.
